question: Implement a generic identity function that returns its argument with the exact same type.
thoughtProcess: The point is to preserve the input type rather than widen it. A type parameter T inferred from the argument lets the return type equal the input type. Avoid using 'any', which would erase the type. The generic should be inferred at the call site so callers get back exactly what they passed.
lineByLine: Line 1 declares a generic parameter T and types both the parameter and return as T, so the compiler infers T from the argument. Line 2 returns the value unchanged. The call sites show T inferred per call. The arrow form uses <T,> with a trailing comma to disambiguate from JSX in .tsx files.

alternativeApproaches.title: Constrained identity
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a constraint when you only want to accept certain shapes while still echoing the precise type.
alternativeApproaches.code: function identityObj<T extends object>(v: T): T { return v; }

followUps.question: Why not type it as (value: any) => any?
followUps.answer: any loses the input type; callers would get any back, defeating type safety and autocomplete. The generic preserves the exact type.

question: Implement a generic, type-safe Stack<T> class with push, pop, peek, size, and isEmpty.
thoughtProcess: I want a container parameterized by element type T so push only accepts T and pop returns T | undefined. Internal storage is a private T[]. pop and peek must account for emptiness, so their return type is T | undefined. Keeping the array private enforces the LIFO discipline through the public API.
lineByLine: The class declares type parameter T. items is a private T[] initialized empty. push takes a T and appends it. pop delegates to Array.pop, whose type is already T | undefined. peek reads the last element, also possibly undefined. size is a getter returning the count. isEmpty returns a boolean. Instantiating with <number> binds T so the whole API is number-typed.
timeComplexity: O(1) per push/pop/peek (amortized for array growth)

alternativeApproaches.title: Linked-list backing
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use nodes for guaranteed O(1) push/pop without array reallocation, at the cost of more memory per node.
alternativeApproaches.code: type Node<T> = { value: T; next: Node<T> | null };

alternativeApproaches.title: Readonly snapshot
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Expose a toArray(): readonly T[] for inspection without leaking the mutable internal array.
alternativeApproaches.code: toArray(): readonly T[] { return [...this.items]; }

followUps.question: How would you make pop throw instead of returning undefined?
followUps.answer: Add a guard: if (this.isEmpty()) throw new Error('empty'); then narrow the return to T. Returning T | undefined vs throwing is an API design choice.

question: Implement a typed pluck<T, K extends keyof T> that extracts one property's values from an array of objects.
thoughtProcess: I want the key constrained to actual keys of T using K extends keyof T, and the return element type to be the indexed access type T[K]. This makes both the key argument autocomplete and the result type precise. The function maps each element to obj[key].
lineByLine: The signature constrains K to keyof T, so only real property names are accepted. The return type T[K][] is an array of the indexed access type, giving the precise value type per key. The body maps each item to item[key]. Calls infer T from the array and K from the literal key, so 'name' yields string[] and an invalid key fails to compile.

alternativeApproaches.title: Pluck multiple keys
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Generalize to several keys using a tuple of keys and Pick to type the result rows.

followUps.question: What is T[K] called?
followUps.answer: An indexed access (lookup) type. It retrieves the type of property K on T, and distributes if K is a union of keys.

question: Implement Partial<T> from scratch as a mapped type.
thoughtProcess: Partial makes every property optional. I iterate over the keys of T with a mapped type [P in keyof T], add the optional modifier '?', and keep the original property type via the lookup T[P]. The result is a new type with all properties optional.
lineByLine: The mapped type iterates P over every key in keyof T. The '?' adds the optional modifier to each mapped property. T[P] keeps each property's original type. Applying it to User yields all-optional fields, so a partial patch object type-checks.

alternativeApproaches.title: DeepPartial
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Recurse into nested objects to make everything optional at all depths.
alternativeApproaches.code: type DeepPartial<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] extends object ? DeepPartial<T[P]> : T[P] };

alternativeApproaches.title: Remove optionality
alternativeApproaches.explanation: The inverse uses the -? modifier to make properties required (Required<T>).
alternativeApproaches.code: type MyRequired<T> = { [P in keyof T]-?: T[P] };

followUps.question: How would you make only some keys optional?
followUps.answer: Combine Pick/Omit with Partial: type PartialBy<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K> & Partial<Pick<T, K>>.

question: Implement Pick<T, K extends keyof T> from scratch.
thoughtProcess: Pick keeps only the keys named in K. I constrain K to keyof T, then build a mapped type iterating P over K (not over keyof T), copying each T[P]. Because P ranges only over the selected keys, the result contains exactly those properties.
lineByLine: K is constrained to keyof T so only valid keys are allowed. The mapped type iterates P over the union K, and T[P] copies each selected property's type. Picking 'id' | 'name' from User produces a type with just those two properties.

alternativeApproaches.title: Omit via Pick + Exclude
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Omit is the complement; implement it by picking all keys except K.
alternativeApproaches.code: type MyOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = MyPick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;

followUps.question: Why iterate over K instead of keyof T?
followUps.answer: Iterating over K restricts the output to exactly the requested keys; iterating keyof T would require filtering and not narrow the result the same way.

question: Implement Readonly<T> from scratch.
thoughtProcess: Readonly adds the readonly modifier to every property. A mapped type over keyof T with the 'readonly' keyword prefix and the original T[P] value type does it. The result prevents reassignment of any property at compile time.
lineByLine: The mapped type iterates P over keyof T and prefixes each mapped property with the readonly modifier. T[P] preserves the value type. Applying it to Point makes both x and y immutable, so assigning p.x is a compile error.

alternativeApproaches.title: Strip readonly
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use the -readonly modifier to produce a mutable version (Mutable<T>).
alternativeApproaches.code: type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P] };

alternativeApproaches.title: Deep readonly
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Recurse for nested immutability.
alternativeApproaches.code: type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[P]> : T[P] };

followUps.question: Is readonly enforced at runtime?
followUps.answer: No, it's compile-time only; the emitted JS has no enforcement. Use Object.freeze for runtime immutability.

question: Implement DeepPartial<T> that makes every property optional recursively, including nested objects and arrays.
thoughtProcess: I make each property optional with '?', then conditionally recurse: if the property is an object (and not a function), apply DeepPartial again; otherwise keep it. Arrays need handling so their elements become DeepPartial too. I'll branch on array-ness before the general object case to avoid mangling array element types.
lineByLine: First a conditional excludes functions (return them as-is so call signatures aren't mapped). Next, arrays are detected with 'infer U' and their element type is recursively DeepPartial'd. Then plain objects map each key optional and recurse via DeepPartial<T[P]>. The final branch returns primitives unchanged. The example shows a deeply partial config where only one nested field is supplied.

alternativeApproaches.title: Simpler non-array version
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If you don't need array element recursion, a smaller version suffices.
alternativeApproaches.code: type DeepPartialSimple<T> = { [P in keyof T]?: T[P] extends object ? DeepPartialSimple<T[P]> : T[P] };

followUps.question: Why exclude functions first?
followUps.answer: Functions are objects too; without the guard the mapped type would iterate their (rarely meaningful) properties and break call signatures.

question: Implement a type-safe groupBy that groups an array by a key selector and returns a typed record.
thoughtProcess: The selector returns a grouping key constrained to PropertyKey (string | number | symbol). The result is a Record from that key type to arrays of the element type. I accumulate into an object, creating empty arrays lazily. Typing the accumulator as Partial<Record<K, T[]>> keeps it honest while building, then I assert the final shape.
lineByLine: T is the element type, K the grouping key constrained to PropertyKey. The return is Record<K, T[]>. result starts as an empty object asserted to the record type. For each item the key is computed; result[key] ??= [] creates the bucket if missing, then pushes the item. Calling with a selector returning p.city infers K as string and groups people into city buckets.

alternativeApproaches.title: Map-backed
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use a Map<K, T[]> to support object/non-string keys and preserve insertion order cleanly.

followUps.question: Why constrain K to PropertyKey?
followUps.answer: Record keys must be string, number, or symbol; PropertyKey is exactly that union, so it rejects keys that can't index an object.

question: Implement a typed event emitter where event names map to specific payload types.
thoughtProcess: I define an events map type (event name -> payload). on, off, and emit are generic over K extends keyof Events, so the listener and emitted payload are typed per event. Internally I store handler arrays keyed by event name. The key trick is using K extends keyof Events to tie the payload type to the event name.
lineByLine:
Listener

is a function taking a payload P. The Emitter is parameterized by an Events map. handlers is a mapped type holding optional arrays of listeners per event. on/off/emit are each generic over K extends keyof Events; Events[K] looks up the payload type for that event so the listener and emit payload match exactly. on lazily creates the array and pushes; off filters out the handler; emit invokes each handler with the typed payload. With AppEvents, 'login' handlers receive { userId: string }.
timeComplexity: O(1) register, O(m) emit for m handlers, O(m) off

alternativeApproaches.title: once + unsubscribe handle
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Return an unsubscribe function from on for ergonomic cleanup, and add once that auto-removes.
alternativeApproaches.code: on<K extends keyof Events>(e: K, fn: Listener<Events[K]>): () => void { (this.handlers[e] ??= []).push(fn); return () => this.off(e, fn); }

followUps.question: How does emit know the payload type?
followUps.answer: emit is generic over K; once the literal event name fixes K, Events[K] resolves to that event's payload type, so passing the wrong shape is a compile error.

question: Narrow a discriminated union with a switch and enforce exhaustiveness at compile time.
thoughtProcess: Each variant shares a literal discriminant (kind). A switch on that discriminant narrows to each variant in its case. To guarantee all cases are handled, the default case assigns the value to a variable of type never; if a new variant is added and unhandled, that assignment fails to compile, catching the gap.
lineByLine: Shape is a union discriminated by the literal 'kind'. assertNever takes never and throws, used as the exhaustiveness sentinel. In area, switching on shape.kind narrows shape to the matching variant in each case, so shape.radius/side/w are accessible only where valid. The default passes shape to assertNever; if every case is handled, shape is narrowed to never and compiles. Add a new variant without a case and shape is no longer never, producing a compile error.

alternativeApproaches.title: Record dispatch
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Map each kind to a handler in a typed record to force exhaustiveness via the Record key set.
alternativeApproaches.code: const handlers: Record<Shape['kind'], (s: any) => number> = { circle: (s) => Math.PI * s.radius ** 2, square: (s) => s.side ** 2, rect: (s) => s.w * s.h };

followUps.question: Why does the never trick work?
followUps.answer: After all variants are handled, control-flow narrows the value to never; assigning never to a never parameter is fine. An unhandled variant leaves a non-never type that isn't assignable to never, so it errors.

question: Implement a typed debounce<T extends (...args: any[]) => void> that preserves the original parameter types.
thoughtProcess: Debounce delays invoking the function until a quiet period passes. To keep types, constrain T to a void-returning function and type the returned wrapper's parameters with Parameters<T>. I store a timer id, clear it on each call, and set a new timeout that applies the latest args. Returning void matches T's contract.
lineByLine: T is constrained to a function returning void. The returned wrapper takes ...args: Parameters<T>, so its parameter list mirrors fn's exactly. timer holds the pending timeout, typed with ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> for cross-environment correctness (number in browser, Timeout in Node). On each call it clears any pending timer and schedules a new one that calls fn with the latest args after delayMs. The debouncedLog call enforces (string, number) at compile time.

alternativeApproaches.title: Leading edge / cancel
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add a leading-edge option and a cancel method by returning an object or augmenting the function.
alternativeApproaches.code: type Debounced<T extends (...a: any[]) => void> = ((...a: Parameters<T>) => void) & { cancel: () => void };

alternativeApproaches.title: Preserve return via Promise
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For functions whose result matters, resolve a Promise<ReturnType<T>> on the trailing call instead of returning void.

followUps.question: Why ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> instead of number?
followUps.answer: setTimeout returns a number in browsers but a Timeout object in Node; using ReturnType keeps the code portable across both type environments.

question: Implement MyReturnType<T> using the infer keyword.
thoughtProcess: ReturnType extracts a function's return type. I write a conditional type: if T is a function with some return R, infer R and yield it; otherwise fall back to never (or any). The infer keyword introduces R as a type variable captured from the matched position.
lineByLine: The conditional checks whether T matches the function shape (...args: any[]) => infer R. infer R binds R to whatever the function returns. If T is a function, the type resolves to R; otherwise to never. Applying it to typeof makeUser extracts the object return type; on () => string it gives string; on a non-function (number) it falls through to never.

alternativeApproaches.title: MyParameters with infer
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use infer in the parameter position to capture the argument tuple.
alternativeApproaches.code: type MyParameters<T> = T extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;

alternativeApproaches.title: Awaited-style unwrapping
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Recurse with infer to unwrap Promise return types for async functions.
alternativeApproaches.code: type AsyncReturn<T> = MyReturnType<T> extends Promise<infer V> ? V : MyReturnType<T>;

followUps.question: What does infer actually do?
followUps.answer: It declares a fresh type variable within a conditional type's extends clause and binds it to the type the compiler unifies at that position, letting you extract pieces of a type.

question: Implement a typed Result<T, E> (success/failure) with ok/err helpers and a type guard.
thoughtProcess: Result models success or failure without throwing. I use a discriminated union on an 'ok' boolean: success carries value: T, failure carries error: E. ok() and err() construct each variant. An isOk type guard narrows the union so the caller can safely access value or error. This is the Rust-style errors-as-values pattern.
lineByLine: Result is a discriminated union on the literal 'ok'. ok() builds the success variant typed Result<T, never> so it composes anywhere E is expected; err() mirrors it as Result<never, E>. isOk is a user-defined type guard (r is { ok: true; value: T }) that narrows based on r.ok. parseIntSafe returns err or ok depending on parsing. In the consumer, isOk(r) narrows r so r.value is a number in the true branch and r.error is a string in the false branch.

alternativeApproaches.title: map/unwrap helpers
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add chaining utilities to transform success values while passing errors through.
alternativeApproaches.code: function map<T, U, E>(r: Result<T, E>, f: (v: T) => U): Result<U, E> { return r.ok ? ok(f(r.value)) : r; }

followUps.question: Why use Result over throwing?
followUps.answer: It makes failure part of the type signature, forcing callers to handle errors and enabling exhaustive, type-checked control flow instead of relying on catch blocks.

question: Write a type guard isString and show how it narrows an unknown value.
thoughtProcess: A type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate 'x is string'. Inside, I do the runtime check typeof x === 'string'. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the argument to string in the calling scope, which lets me safely use string methods.
lineByLine: isString takes unknown and returns the type predicate value is string; its body does the runtime typeof check. In printUpper the parameter starts as unknown. Inside the if (isString(value)) branch, the compiler narrows value to string, so value.toUpperCase() is allowed. The else branch keeps value as unknown.

alternativeApproaches.title: Generic array guard
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Build guards for arrays of a checked element type by combining Array.isArray with element checks.
alternativeApproaches.code: function isStringArray(v: unknown): v is string[] { return Array.isArray(v) && v.every(isString); }

followUps.question: What's the difference between a type guard and a cast?
followUps.answer: A guard performs a real runtime check and the predicate reflects it, so narrowing is sound. A cast (as string) asserts without checking and can be wrong, causing runtime errors.

question: Implement a typed fetchJson<T> that returns a typed parsed response.
thoughtProcess: fetchJson should be generic over the expected shape T and return Promise<T>. Since the network boundary is untyped, I should be honest that T is an assertion about the runtime data; ideally a validator runs, but at minimum I type the parsed result as T. I also handle non-2xx responses by throwing. I avoid 'any' by using the generic and casting only the validated boundary.
lineByLine: fetchJson is generic over T and returns Promise<T>. It awaits fetch and throws on non-ok status. res.json() is typed as unknown to acknowledge the data is untrusted, then asserted to T at the boundary. The comment flags that a real validator (e.g. Zod) should replace the assertion for runtime safety. loadUser specializes T to User, so callers get a typed user.
timeComplexity: O(n) in response size for parsing

alternativeApproaches.title: Runtime validation
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Pass a validator/schema and parse the unknown data so the type T is actually verified at runtime, not just asserted.

followUps.question: Is 'data as T' safe?
followUps.answer: No, it's an unchecked assertion; if the server returns a different shape it compiles but fails at runtime. Use a schema validator for true safety at the I/O boundary.

question: Implement a const-assertion-based enum alternative with derived value and key union types.
thoughtProcess: Instead of a runtime enum, I define a plain object with 'as const' so values keep their literal types and are readonly. I then derive the value-union type with typeof obj[keyof typeof obj] and the key-union with keyof typeof obj. This gives enum-like typing with transparent, tree-shakeable JavaScript and no runtime enum object overhead.
lineByLine: Direction is a plain object literal with 'as const', which freezes the values to their string literal types and makes properties readonly. The Direction type uses typeof Direction (the object's type) indexed by keyof typeof Direction to produce the union of its values. DirectionKey is the union of property names. move accepts the value union, so Direction.Up passes while an unknown string fails. There is no emitted enum object beyond the plain const, keeping output minimal and tree-shakeable.

alternativeApproaches.title: Array + index
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Derive a union from a const-asserted array when you only need values, not named keys.
alternativeApproaches.code:
const DIRS = ['UP', 'DOWN', 'LEFT', 'RIGHT'] as const;
type Dir = (typeof DIRS)[number];

alternativeApproaches.title: Native enum
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A regular enum gives the same nominal feel but emits a runtime object and resists tree-shaking.
alternativeApproaches.code: enum DirectionEnum { Up = 'UP', Down = 'DOWN' }

followUps.question: Why prefer this over a native enum?
followUps.answer: It produces plain, debuggable, tree-shakeable JS, works under isolatedModules, and keeps value and type in sync from a single source, whereas enums emit extra runtime objects (and reverse maps for numeric enums).
